slides.text:
A function can call itself. Each call gets its own copy of the parameters and works on a smaller version of the problem, until a case so small it needs no more calls. You will count down, multiply, add and trace what runs when.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
solve(problem):
    if the problem is tiny:
        give the answer
    otherwise:
        solve(a smaller problem)

slides.text:
A recursive function has two parts. The **base case** stops the calls and answers directly. The **recursive case** calls the same function with a smaller input.

The snippet is pseudo code.
Without a base case the calls never stop. The input must also get closer to the base case with every call, or the function runs forever.

exercises.title: Count down
exercises.guide: Print a number, then let the function call itself with a smaller one.

chunks.guide: The `if` is the base case: it ends the calls. The `else` calls the same function with a smaller number.

exercises.title: Multiply down to one
exercises.guide: Multiply a number by the factorial of the one below it.

chunks.guide: The package and the import are already in the file. The base case returns a value, and the other case uses the value of the smaller call.

exercises.title: Add down to zero
exercises.guide: Fill the value of the base case and the name of the function that calls itself.

exercises.title: Raise to a power
exercises.guide: Multiply the base by the same power, one step lower.

chunks.guide: Only `exp` shrinks. `base` goes along unchanged in every call.
Anything raised to 0 is 1, which is why the base case returns 1.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: `halve(9)` calls `halve(4)`, then `halve(2)`, then `halve(1)`, which returns 0. Three calls each add 1, so the result is 3. `halve(1)` hits the base case at once and returns 0.

slides.text:
Code placed **before** the recursive call runs on the way in. Code placed **after** it waits, and runs on the way back out, once the deeper call has finished.

The snippet is pseudo code.
slides.code:
f(n):
    if n > 0:
        before(n)
        f(n - 1)
        after(n)

slides.text: A function can also call itself **twice**. Each of those calls makes two more, so the number of calls grows quickly. The answer still comes from the same two parts: a base case, and the results of the smaller calls combined.

exercises.title: In and out
exercises.guide: Print before the call and after it, and see the order.

chunks.guide: The package and the import are already in the file. The line after the call waits until the deeper calls are done.

notes.text: Everything below waits for this call.

chunks.guide: Calls go in with 3, 2, 1 and come out in the opposite order.

output.text:
in 3
in 2
in 1
out 1
out 2
out 3

exercises.title: Greatest common divisor
exercises.guide: Find the largest number that divides both inputs.

chunks.guide: Euclid's rule: the answer for `a` and `b` is the answer for `b` and the remainder of `a` divided by `b`. It stops when `b` reaches 0.

exercises.title: Add the digits
exercises.guide: Fill the operator that takes the last digit, and the comparison that stops the calls.

exercises.title: Two calls at once
exercises.guide: Add the two previous numbers of the sequence.

chunks.guide: Each number is the sum of the two before it. The function calls itself twice, and 0 and 1 are the base cases.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output. Each number is printed on its own line.
exercises.explanation: The print comes after the recursive call, so nothing is printed until the deepest call, `up(1)`, finishes. The numbers come out as the calls return: 1, then 2, then 3.
